teaching.read: Going quiet and doing the bare minimum is almost never laziness; it is usually a retreat to a floor they know they can hold. They have likely decided at some level that full effort followed by failure is worse than low effort followed by a shrug. The belonging angle is that disengagement can also be a way of becoming invisible, staying off the radar of comparison with peers who seem to be doing fine.

pull.instinct: Back off, lower expectations, and wait for them to come around on their own, which signals that you have noticed they are struggling and have quietly given up on them too.

teaching.mentorMove: Name what you see without making it an accusation, and make it clear the floor is not actually safe because you are not going to let them stay there. Hold the full standard while making it clear you are going to help them get there, not just watch.
holdFirm: Full engagement is still the expectation, not the bare minimum.
They do not get to disappear from your attention by going through the motions.
stayFlexible: Where they start re-engaging, whether that is one small piece or something they actually care about.
How openly they talk about what is going on versus what they show through their work.

script.words: Hey, I have been watching you and I want you to know I see you in there. You have not checked out completely, which tells me something.
But something has shifted and I would rather hear it from you than guess. What is the part that feels pointless right now, or too hard, or just not worth it?
I am not asking so I can fix it for you or pretend the work goes away. I am asking because I want to find the crack where we can get you back into this for real, even if it is small at first.

I am holding you to more than this because this is not your ceiling, it is just where you landed when something got heavy. I have seen enough to know the difference, and I am not letting you convince me this is all you have got.

teaching.longGame: The habit you want to build in them over time is the one where struggle does not mean retreat. When they learn that hitting a wall is a signal to ask for traction rather than a reason to stop pushing, they carry that into every hard thing that comes after this.

teaching.read: Going quiet and doing just enough to stay invisible usually means they have decided effort is too risky: if they try and still fail, they lose status in their own eyes. The bare minimum is a controlled burn, not laziness. There is also a belonging signal here: they may feel they have already drifted outside the circle where trying feels normal or safe.

pull.instinct: Leave them alone because pressing feels unkind and at least they are not disrupting anyone, but that silence reads as confirmation that nobody notices or expects more from them, and the drift deepens.

teaching.mentorMove: Break the invisibility without making it a performance review. Go to them briefly, name what you see without judgment, and signal that you are curious about them specifically, not just their output.
holdFirm: The standard for engagement stays the same as it is for everyone else.
You will keep checking in rather than waiting for them to come to you.
stayFlexible: How they show what they know, not just the one default format.
The entry point back in, starting with something they can succeed at quickly.

script.words: Hey, I have noticed you have been quieter than usual lately. I am not saying that as a complaint. I am saying it because I actually pay attention to you.
I am not going to pretend I know what is going on, so I would rather just ask. Is there a part of this that is feeling stuck, or is it something else altogether?
If there is a piece of this that is harder than it looks, let us figure out where to get some traction. I am not looking for perfect right now, I am looking for you back in the game.

I am going to keep checking in, not because I think something is wrong with you but because I have high standards for what you are capable of and I have seen enough to know you can meet them. That does not go away just because things got quiet for a bit.

teaching.longGame: The real lesson is that struggle is not a sign to pull back, it is the moment to reach out. If they learn that going quiet gets them noticed with warmth instead of pressure or silence, they start to trust that effort in a hard stretch is worth something.

teaching.read: Going quiet and coasting is almost never laziness; it is usually a bet that staying small is safer than trying and failing in front of people who matter. Somewhere along the way the cost of visible effort started feeling higher than the cost of invisible disengagement. The status angle is real: doing nothing protects them from the exposure of trying hard and still coming up short.

pull.instinct: Leave them alone because at least they are not disrupting anything and pushing might make it worse, which lets the drift harden into a habit and signals that you have quietly lowered the bar for them.

teaching.mentorMove: Make contact before the gap gets wider, not to interrogate the disengagement but to name what you see without judgment and ask one real question about what is in the way. The standard stays, the pressure comes off the performance and goes onto the conversation.
holdFirm: Full effort and full presence are still the expectation.
Coasting is not a long-term option you will pretend not to notice.
stayFlexible: How they re-enter, whether that is a small task first or jumping back in at full pace.
When and where you check in, so it does not feel like surveillance.

script.words: Hey, I have been noticing you lately and I just wanted a second with you. Nothing bad, I just want to check in.
It feels like you have pulled back a little. I am not going to make a big thing of it, I just want to know honestly what is going on for you right now. What is making this feel not worth the effort?
Whatever it is, let us figure out what one thing would make it feel less stuck. It does not have to be everything at once. What is the smallest move that would feel real to you?

I am going to keep showing up and I need you to keep showing up too. I am holding you to that because I have genuinely high expectations for you and I am not saying that to fill space. I think you are more capable than what I have been seeing, and I want to find out I am right.

teaching.longGame: The goal is for them to learn that struggle is not a verdict on their ability, it is their brain doing harder work than it has done before. The more times they re-engage after going quiet and find out they can handle what was in front of them, the less they will need to disappear when things get hard.

parenting.read: Going quiet and doing the bare minimum is almost never laziness. It is usually a young person who has decided, somewhere beneath the surface, that trying and failing in front of you is worse than not trying at all. The silence is self-protection. The identity piece shows up in the background: they may be quietly asking whether any of this connects to who they actually want to become, and if the answer is unclear, effort feels pointless.

pull.instinct: Give them space, lower the bar, stop pushing because you do not want to add pressure to someone who already looks depleted. This removes the friction but also removes the message that you believe they have more in them, which is exactly what they need to hear.

parenting.mentorMove: Hold the standard where it is, but get curious about what the withdrawal is covering. You are not looking to catch them being lazy; you are looking for the spot where confidence broke down, and that conversation has to happen one to one with no audience and no agenda except finding out.
holdFirm: The minimum is not the ceiling and you are not going to pretend it is.
You staying in the relationship, paying attention, is not optional just because they have gone quiet.
stayFlexible: Where and when you have this conversation, on their terms if possible.
How they show you effort, not whether they show it.

script.words: I am not going to make this into a big confrontation. I just have noticed you have been quieter than usual, and I miss you in this, honestly. I want to know what is going on with you.

I am not asking about the work right now. I am asking about you. What does this feel like from where you are standing? Is there something that has started to feel pointless, or hard, or like it is not worth the risk?

Here is what I want to try. You tell me one thing that would make this feel like it matters, even a little, and I will work with that. I am not locked in to things being exactly the way they are. What I am locked in to is you not disappearing on me.

I am not dropping the expectation, because I do not actually think you are someone who is fine with coasting. I think something got in the way of you believing you could do more than the minimum, and I am holding you to the higher standard because I have seen what you are capable of and I am not willing to pretend I have not.

parenting.longGame: The habit you are building in them is the one that matters most later: when something feels impossible or pointless, the move is to say so to someone who can help, not to quietly shrink. Young people who learn to name the stall and ask for what they need become adults who push through hard stretches instead of waiting for someone to notice they have stopped.

parenting.read: Going quiet and doing the bare minimum is rarely laziness; it is usually a signal that something feels too risky to try at full effort. If they put everything in and it still is not enough, that is a devastating verdict on who they are becoming. Pulling back protects them from that verdict. The bare minimum is a way of saying the game is not worth playing, which often means they do not believe they can win it.

pull.instinct: Stop pushing to avoid making things worse, which feels kind but confirms to them that you have also concluded they cannot handle more.

parenting.mentorMove: Hold the expectation that they show up and engage, while making it safe to admit out loud that something feels stuck. The conversation has to come before the performance does.
holdFirm: Showing up and doing real work is not optional.
You will not pretend the withdrawal is fine just to keep the peace.
stayFlexible: Where they start, and how big the first step needs to be.
Whether they talk to you about what is stuck or find another person they trust to say it to first.

script.words: I have noticed you have gone quiet lately, and I want you to know I am not coming at you about it. I just miss you being in it.
When something starts to feel like it is not worth trying, there is usually a reason. Not a bad reason, just a reason. What does it feel like from the inside right now?

I am not asking you to fix everything today. I am asking us to figure out together what one thing would make it feel slightly less pointless, because I do not think you have actually stopped caring. I think something made caring feel dangerous.

I am holding you to showing up fully, not because I need to check a box, but because I have watched you do hard things and I know your brain is more capable than what you are letting it do right now. That is the standard, and you are the reason I believe you can get back there.

parenting.longGame: The habit you are building here is not compliance, it is self-rescue: learning to name when something feels stuck instead of disappearing into it, so they never have to white-knuckle their way back alone. That skill will matter in every room they ever sit in.

parenting.read: Going quiet and doing the bare minimum is almost never laziness; it is self-protection. If they do not try, they cannot fail in a way that says something damning about who they are. Something has made them doubt whether they can actually do this, and the retreat is them managing that threat before it lands publicly. The identity piece is underneath it: they are quietly working out whether this thing, and maybe the kind of person who does it, is even them anymore.

pull.instinct: Lower the expectation or stop pushing to avoid adding more pressure, which tells them you have already decided they cannot handle it and makes the withdrawal feel permanently justified.

parenting.mentorMove: Hold the standard exactly where it was, but go toward the quiet instead of waiting it out. Name what you see without judgment, ask what is actually hard, and make it plain that struggle is what working at the edge of your ability looks like, not a sign you are in the wrong place.
holdFirm: They stay engaged and keep showing up, not just occupying space.
The minimum goes up, not sideways, from here.
stayFlexible: How they show what they know or what they are working on.
How much they talk to you versus work it through first on their own.

script.words: I am not coming at you about this. I just notice you have gone somewhere I cannot see, and I miss you in it.
Something shifted. I do not know if it was one moment or a slow buildup, but I want to understand it before I say another word about expectations. What does this feel like from the inside right now?

Here is what I know about the quiet, barely-there version of you: it shows up when something feels like it might prove a bad thing about you if you actually go for it. That is your brain doing its job, but it is protecting you from the wrong thing. The risk worth taking is not playing small and wondering. Let us figure out together what the first real step looks like, not the whole mountain.

I am not pulling back what I expect from you, because I am not willing to decide you cannot do this just because it is hard right now. Your brain is building something when it struggles, not breaking. I am holding you to more than the minimum because I have seen what you are capable of and I am not letting either of us forget it.

parenting.longGame: The habit you are building in them is learning to stay in the room when something gets hard instead of going through the motions until the discomfort passes. People who can do that, who can name what is scaring them and take the next step anyway, are the ones who eventually trust their own capability, and that trust is what no grade or outcome can give them.

managing.read: Going quiet and doing the minimum is rarely laziness; it is usually someone who has decided, privately, that trying and failing is worse than not trying at all. They may have hit something hard, gotten feedback that landed wrong, or looked around and concluded they are behind where they should be. The bare minimum is armor. Underneath it is someone unsure whether they can actually do this job, and that question is starting to feel like it might answer itself in the wrong direction.

pull.instinct: Leave them alone and hope they come around on their own, which lets the story in their head harden into fact and makes you complicit in their stalling out.

managing.mentorMove: Go to them directly and name what you are seeing without turning it into an accusation. The goal is to crack the door open so they can say what is actually going on, then reconnect the work to something that matters to them specifically.
holdFirm: The standard of contribution stays the same regardless of what is going on internally.
They do not get to disappear into the background on your watch.
stayFlexible: What they work on first to get their footing back.
Whether they rebuild through a visible win, a quieter project, or a short conversation with you each week.

script.words: I noticed you have been pretty heads down lately, and I am not saying that as a complaint. I just know the difference between someone who is focused and someone who has gone quiet for a different reason, and I want to check in.
Is there something about the work right now that feels stuck, or not worth the effort, or just not clicking? I am not asking to evaluate you. I am asking because the answer changes what we do next.

Tell me what part of this role, even a small part, felt like it actually meant something when you first came in. Because I think we can find a way to get you more of that and less of whatever has been draining the life out of the last few weeks.

I am going to hold you to showing up fully, not because I need bodies in chairs, but because I think you are capable of doing work here that actually matters and I am not willing to watch you undersell that. Let us figure out what gets you back there.

managing.longGame: The skill you are building in them is the ability to name when they are struggling before the struggle becomes a crisis. People who can do that are the ones who get trusted with harder things, because their manager is never the last to know.

managing.read: Going quiet and doing the bare minimum is almost never laziness; it is self-protection. Something made them doubt whether they can actually succeed here, and pulling back limits how exposed they are. The identity layer shows up because early-career workers are still figuring out whether they are the kind of person who belongs in a professional environment, and if the evidence is starting to feel like no, shutting down is less frightening than trying and confirming the fear.

pull.instinct: Let it slide and assume they will come around on their own, which signals that the standard was optional and leaves them alone with whatever is blocking them.

managing.mentorMove: Name what you are noticing without framing it as a complaint, and get curious before you get corrective. Your job is to find out what they have lost confidence in, not to push harder on output before you know what is in the way.
holdFirm: The level of contribution you expect from them stays the same.
The conversation happens, even if they would rather avoid it.
stayFlexible: What they work on first to rebuild momentum.
How much check-in contact they get while they are finding their footing again.

script.words: I am not pulling you in here to put you on the spot. I just notice you have gone quieter lately and I would rather ask you about it than pretend I did not.

What is going on for you right now? Not the professional answer, the real one. Is there a part of the work that has started to feel like it is not going anywhere, or something that got harder without a lot of explanation?

Tell me what would make it easier to come back in, and I will tell you honestly what I can move and what stays the same. I would rather build a path through this with you than watch you coast through something you are capable of more than.

I am holding you to a higher level than what I have been seeing, and I want to be straight with you about why: I think you have more range than you are using right now, and I do not want to watch you spend this stretch of your career in first gear. Let us figure out what it looks like to actually show up here.

managing.longGame: What they are learning is whether struggle means stop or means something harder is coming that they can handle. Your job over time is to make enough of the wins visible that their internal evidence starts pointing toward capable rather than exposed.

managing.read: Going quiet and doing the minimum is almost never laziness. It usually means they have decided at some level that trying and falling short is more dangerous to how they see themselves than simply not trying. The bare minimum is a controlled outcome. If they never fully engage, they never fully fail. There is also an identity question underneath: they may not yet see this work as connected to who they are becoming, which makes it easy to treat as something to get through rather than something to get good at.

pull.instinct: Let it ride and hope they come around on their own, because pushing someone who is already withdrawn feels like it will make things worse and create an awkward dynamic.

managing.mentorMove: Go to them before the silence becomes the norm. Name what you are seeing without judgment, get genuinely curious about what is getting in the way, and connect the work to something they actually care about being or becoming.
holdFirm: The standard of work does not drop because they are going through something.
They stay in the conversation about how to get there, not out of it.
stayFlexible: What the path back to full engagement looks like and at what pace.
Which part of the work they can lean into first to rebuild momentum.

script.words: I have noticed you have been pretty quiet lately and keeping things at arm's length. I am not here to put you on the spot. I just do not want to let it sit there without checking in.

What is going on for you right now? Not a performance review, just a real question. Is it the work itself, something about the situation here, something outside of work? I would rather know than guess.

Tell me what part of this job, if any, actually interests you or connects to where you want to be in a few years. I am asking because I want to figure out how to make the work worth putting real effort into, not just worth showing up for.

Here is what I need from you going forward: full effort, not perfection. I am holding you to that because I think you have more in you than what I have been seeing, and I would rather say that directly than watch you stay smaller than you are.

managing.longGame: The habit you are building in them is learning to stay in the room when things feel uncertain rather than shrinking down to minimum safe output. People who can stay engaged when they are not sure they will succeed are the ones who actually develop. That is the capacity worth going after here.

coaching.read: Going quiet and doing just enough to stay invisible usually means they have decided that trying hard and coming up short is worse than not trying at all. The bare minimum is armor, not laziness. Underneath it is probably a question they are not asking out loud: what if I actually put in the work and it still does not go well. The belonging thread is that pulling back from the group keeps them from being seen struggling in front of peers.

pull.instinct: Leave them alone and hope they come around on their own, which feels kind but actually confirms that you have written them off too.

coaching.mentorMove: Go to them privately, name what you are seeing without making it an accusation, and make the standard visible again alongside a genuine statement that you believe they are capable of meeting it. The goal is to close the distance before the disconnection becomes a habit.
holdFirm: Full effort in practice is still the expectation, not optional.
Checking in with you when something is off is part of being on this team.
stayFlexible: How much you share with the rest of the group about where they are.
What doing full effort looks like for them right now, physically and emotionally.

script.words: Hey, walk with me a second. I am not pulling you aside to get on you. I just want to actually talk to you.
Something has shifted and I noticed it. You are here, you are doing what you have to do, and that is it. I am not going to pretend I did not see that. What is going on?

If something about this feels like it is not worth your energy right now, I want to know what that is. Not so I can argue you out of it, but because if there is something I can adjust in how we are working together, that is a real conversation I am willing to have.

What I am not going to do is let you disappear in the middle of this group. I have high standards for you specifically because I have seen what you can actually do, and I am not dropping that just because things feel flat right now. Your brain is doing exactly what it does when it is trying to figure something hard out. That is not a problem, that is the process.

coaching.longGame: The habit you are building in them is learning that struggle is information, not a verdict. An athlete who can recognize when they are shrinking and bring it to someone they trust instead of going underground with it will recover from setbacks faster and go further than one who only shows up when things feel good.

coaching.read: Going quiet and doing just enough to stay invisible usually means they have decided that trying and falling short in front of everyone is worse than not trying at all. The bare minimum is armor. They are not disengaged from the outcome; they are terrified of what a real attempt might reveal about them, and they would rather be seen as someone who does not care than someone who tried and could not do it.

pull.instinct: Leave them alone because pushing feels cruel when they are already struggling, but that quietly tells them you agree there is not much there to work with, which makes the withdrawal worse.

coaching.mentorMove: Break the silence without making it a production. Get alongside them in a low-stakes moment and say directly that you see them and you are not letting them disappear, then give them something small and winnable right now so they can remember what competence feels like before the bigger ask comes.
holdFirm: Full effort is still the expectation, not survival mode.
They stay in the reps, the drills, the meetings, and they engage, not just occupy space.
stayFlexible: How much you spotlight them in front of the group while they are rebuilding.
Which task or role you use to give them an early win.

script.words: Hey, just you and me for a second. I have been watching you and I want you to know I see you in there, even when you are keeping it low.
Something shifted on you. I am not here to call you out for it, I just want to understand. What has been feeling hard lately, even if it is hard to put into words?

Here is what I want to do. I am going to give you one specific thing to own today, something I know is in your range. Not to test you, but because I think getting your hands back on something real will matter more than anything I could say to you right now.

I am not going to let you coast, and that is not a threat, that is because I have high standards for you and I genuinely believe you can meet them. Your brain is not stuck; it is actually getting more capable every time you push through something uncomfortable, and I want you back in that process with me.

coaching.longGame: What they are learning right now, underneath the withdrawal, is whether adults write them off when they go quiet or stay in the relationship. Staying in it teaches them that struggle is a phase you move through with support, not proof that you do not belong here.

coaching.read: Going quiet and doing just enough to survive is almost always a signal that trying hard feels more dangerous than coasting. If they push and fail visibly, that hurts worse than never pushing at all. Underneath that is a status worry too: the group watches, and struggling in front of them carries a cost they may not be willing to pay right now.

pull.instinct: Leave them alone, assume they need space, lower the bar quietly so things stay comfortable, which signals that you have already written off their potential and makes the retreat feel justified.

coaching.mentorMove: Go to them one on one, name what you are seeing without judgment, and make it genuinely safe to say what is hard. Then hold the expectation while making the path back in feel possible rather than humiliating.
holdFirm: Full engagement is still the standard, not survival mode.
They stay in the work with the team rather than disappearing into the edges of it.
stayFlexible: Where they re-enter at full effort, whether that is a smaller role, a specific drill, or a different kind of contribution first.

script.words: Hey, I am not coming at you with a problem. I just want two minutes because I have been watching and I think something is going on that you have not said out loud yet.
What is the part that feels stuck right now? Not the answer you think I want, the real one. Is it something about the work, something about the group, something about where you think you stand?

Because here is what I know: your brain does not go quiet because it is done. It goes quiet because it is trying to protect you from something. That is not weakness, that is actually your system doing its job. So let us figure out what it is protecting you from and build a different way back in.

I am not letting you stay at the edges of this, and that is not pressure for the sake of it. I hold you to more because I have watched what you are capable of and I am not willing to pretend I have not seen it. We do this together.

coaching.longGame: The habit you are trying to build in them is tolerating the discomfort of trying without certainty of success. Every time they stay in the room when it is hard and come out the other side, that tolerance grows. The goal is not this practice or this season; it is a person who does not disappear when things get difficult.

A.read: Before they have done a single thing, they are already calculating whether they can actually succeed here. Showing up on day one without knowing the rules is not just disorienting, it is a status threat disguised as a logistical problem. If the expectations land as a long list of ways to fail, their nervous system will treat the job as a test they are already behind on.

pull.instinct: Front-load every policy, standard, and consequence on day one so nothing is ambiguous, which turns the first day into an audit they cannot possibly pass and teaches them the job is about surviving you rather than building something.

A.mentorMove: Name one or two expectations that actually matter this week, explain why they matter to the work and to the team, and make clear you are the person they come to when they are unsure, not the person they hide from when they slip up.
holdFirm: The core standards apply from day one, not after some grace period.
Asking for help and flagging confusion early is a professional expectation, not optional.
stayFlexible: Which expectations you introduce in week one versus week two or three.
Whether you deliver them in a meeting, a short written summary, or a walk-around where things come up naturally.

script.words: Starting somewhere new is a lot, even when you are excited about it. The first week your brain is doing a lot of work just figuring out where things are and how things move, so I want to make this landing as clean as possible for you.
Before I tell you anything, what feels most uncertain right now? What would make Monday feel less like a guessing game?

Here is what I am going to do. I will give you the two or three things that matter most this week, so you know where to put your attention. Everything else we will build in as you get your footing. And when something is unclear, I want to hear it from you directly before it becomes a problem, because that is how good work actually happens.

I am holding you to a real standard here, not a probationary one, because I would not have hired you if I did not think you could meet it. The standard is the same on day one as it is on day ninety. What changes is how much of the context you have to work with, and that part I am going to make sure you get.

A.longGame: The goal is that by the end of the first month they understand the expectations well enough to explain them to the next new hire. That kind of ownership does not come from a policy handout on day one; it comes from a manager who treated the standards as something worth understanding, not just enforcing.

A.read: Before they have done a single thing, a new hire is already running quiet calculations about whether they can actually succeed here. Walking in on day one to a wall of expectations can land as a signal that the bar is high and they are already behind, which triggers avoidance or people-pleasing instead of genuine engagement. The belonging piece shows up because they are also scanning every interaction for whether they fit the culture and whether anyone actually wants them here.

pull.instinct: Hold back the real standards to avoid overwhelming them, which feels kind but leaves them guessing what good looks like and sets you up to have harder conversations later when the gap is already visible.

A.mentorMove: Name the standards clearly and early, but pair every expectation with the signal that you are going to be in their corner as they grow into it. The goal is not to soften the bar, it is to make sure they know you are not just dropping them at the starting line.
holdFirm: The actual standards for the role do not change because they are new.
They deserve an honest picture of what success looks like, starting now.
stayFlexible: The pace at which different expectations come into full focus during their ramp.
How much structure versus room to figure things out they want in the early weeks.

script.words: I am genuinely glad you are here. Before we get into anything logistical, I want you to know that I remember what week one feels like, and it is a lot. Whatever you are feeling right now is a completely normal response to a brain that is taking in a huge amount of new information at once.
I want to ask you one thing before I share my end: what would make this first stretch feel like it was actually working for you? What does a good start look like from where you sit?

Here is my honest picture of what the role requires and where I will be watching for growth. I am not going to pretend the bar is low, because it is not and you deserve to know that. But I am also telling you that my job is to make sure you have what you need to get there, so if something is unclear or you hit a wall, I want to hear that from you directly.

I am holding you to the real standard from day one because I already believe you can reach it. What I am asking from you is that you tell me when something is not clicking rather than trying to figure it out alone in the dark.

A.longGame: How you introduce expectations on Monday sets the template for how they will handle pressure for the rest of their time working for you. A person who learns early that standards and support come as a package deal will bring you problems while they are still fixable, which is the single most useful habit an early-career employee can build.

A.read: Before they have done a single thing, they are already measuring whether they can cut it here. The first week is less about learning tasks and more about reading every signal for whether they belong or are already behind. If expectations land like a verdict instead of a starting point, they will spend energy hiding confusion rather than asking questions.

pull.instinct: Front-load every standard and policy at once to cover yourself and show you run a tight team, which buries them before they have a foothold and teaches them that this place is about not screwing up, not about growing.

A.mentorMove: Name the one or two things that actually matter most right now, be explicit that everything else comes later, and make clear that asking questions is the job in week one, not a sign they are not ready.
holdFirm: The core expectations you name on day one are real and you will follow up on them.
Asking questions and flagging confusion is required, not optional.
stayFlexible: The order and pace in which everything else gets introduced.
How they prefer to check in with you as they get their footing.

script.words: Welcome, genuinely. Starting somewhere new is a lot, and I remember that the first week feels like you are drinking from a fire hose no matter how prepared you are. That is normal here, not a warning sign.
Before I say anything about expectations, I want to know one thing: what would make this first week feel like a win to you? What would you need to walk out Friday thinking it went well?

Here is what I am going to do. I am going to give you two things that matter most right now and hold off on everything else until you have your feet under you. And I want us to set up a short check-in each day this week, not to grade you but so you have a place to put questions before they pile up.

One thing I will hold you to from day one: when something is unclear, you bring it to me. I have high standards here and I am telling you directly that I think you are capable of meeting them, but I can only help you get there if I know where you are actually at.

A.longGame: How you set up week one determines whether they spend the next six months performing confidence they do not have or building real competence they can stand on. The goal is to make asking questions feel like the smart move, not the risky one, so that when real challenges show up they come to you instead of guessing and hiding.

turn1.read: The stalling is almost never about laziness; it is about not wanting to start something that might prove they cannot do it. The desk becomes a place where their ability gets tested, and the morning drag is the brain buying time before that test begins. There is also a layer of control wrapped in the delay: if they cannot choose whether to do the work, slowing the start is one of the few levers they still own.

pull.instinct: Stand over them, count down, take away screens until they open the book — which turns every morning into a standoff and makes the work feel like punishment rather than something they are capable of.

turn1.mentorMove: Separate the what from the when: the work is not up for debate, but let them have a real hand in deciding exactly how the morning sequences so the start is theirs to own, not yours to force.
holdFirm: The agreed work gets done before the day moves on.
They are the one who opens the book, not you opening it for them.
stayFlexible: What time exactly they sit down within a reasonable window they help pick.
Whether they start with the hardest piece or the easiest, music or silence, ten-minute chunks or a longer stretch.

script.words: I am not here to fight about the mornings. I actually think the stalling is telling me something real, and I would rather know what that is than just keep pushing.

When you sit down and then kind of drift, what is going through your head right then? Is it that you do not know where to start, that it feels like a lot, that it just feels pointless? I am genuinely asking, not setting you up.

So here is what I want to try. You tell me exactly how you would want the morning to run, what time, in what order, and I will hold that schedule with you instead of fighting you into mine. The work stays, but the shape of it is something we can build together.

I am holding you to doing the work every day because I know you are more than capable of it, and I am not willing to let you talk yourself out of proving that. But from here, I want the start of the day to feel like something you chose, not something that happened to you.

turn1.longGame: What you are really building is their ability to begin hard things without someone dragging them to the starting line. That skill shows up on every project, every job, every moment in adult life where no one is watching and the work still has to happen.

turn2.read: Agreeing and then doing nothing is not defiance; it is the competence trap closing shut. The conversation felt manageable, but the actual desk still means the actual test, and when the moment came, avoidance won again. The new wrinkle is that they have now had two chances to fail to start, and that pattern is quietly building a story in their head about whether they are someone who can follow through.

pull.instinct: Let it slide again because at least they agreed and you do not want another hard conversation, which teaches them that agreements with you have no weight and that avoidance always eventually works.

turn2.mentorMove: Stop negotiating the launch and instead shrink the task until the first move is so small it is almost impossible to avoid, then stand close enough to witness them take it, not to police them but to make starting a shared moment rather than a solitary dread.
holdFirm: Work happens today, not after a new agreement about tomorrow.
They take the first visible action while you are still in the room.
stayFlexible: How small the first action is: one problem, one paragraph, one sentence, whatever gets the pen moving.
Whether you sit nearby doing your own thing or step out the moment they are actually going.

script.words: I am not angry, and I am not going to lecture you about yesterday. I know the agreement felt real when we made it, and I know something still got in the way.

I want to ask you something and I need the honest answer: when it was actually time to sit down, what happened in your head right at that moment? Because I do not think you just decided not to bother.

So we are going to try something different right now, not tomorrow morning, right now. You pick one thing, the smallest possible piece of this work, and you do it while I am sitting here. I am not grading you, I am not hovering; I am just going to be in the room so the start is not something you are doing alone in your own head.

I am holding you to this because I have high standards for you and I genuinely believe you can do this work. What I will not do is keep making new plans while the old ones go nowhere, so today we skip the plan and just begin.

turn2.longGame: The goal is not a better morning routine; it is breaking the link between starting hard things and feeling like you might fail at them. Every time they begin and survive it, that link gets a little weaker, and eventually they stop needing you in the room to make it possible.

turn1.read: Stalling almost always means the work feels too hard, too uncertain, or too easy to fail at. Every morning the table is set again for the same quiet fear: what if I sit down and it goes badly. The drag is not laziness; it is their nervous system running out the clock to avoid finding out something uncomfortable about what they can do. The autonomy piece shows up because even work they agreed to can start feeling like something being done to them once the grind of daily repetition sets in.

pull.instinct: Stand over them or keep calling from the other room with rising frustration, which turns every morning into a power contest and makes the work feel even more threatening because now failure is public.

turn1.mentorMove: Name what you are actually seeing, not the stalling but the hesitation underneath it, and give them one small on-ramp that gets them started without requiring them to feel ready first. Then hold the agreement without holding your breath over every minute.
holdFirm: The schoolwork happens every morning, same window, no negotiation on that.
They do the actual thinking themselves; your job is not to sit beside them and smooth every hard part.
stayFlexible: Which task they start with, so they get some say over the door they walk through.
How the first five minutes look, whether that is jotting one idea, reading one paragraph, or just opening the page.

script.words: I have watched you push through things that looked impossible to you at the start and come out the other side. That is a real pattern, not a fluke.

Tell me what is happening in that first stretch in the morning. Not the excuses, the actual feeling. Is it that the work feels too big, too boring, too hard to get a grip on? I genuinely want to know.

Okay, so here is what we can do together. You pick which piece you touch first, even if it is the smallest one. Once you are in, you are in, and I will leave you alone to work. But we are not going to keep letting the morning drain away while the work sits there.

The agreement we made is still the agreement. I am holding you to it not because I want mornings to be a battle but because I know your brain is more than capable of this, and I am not willing to let you talk yourself out of proving that every single day.

turn1.longGame: The habit you are building is not really about schoolwork. It is the ability to start something hard before they feel ready, which is the one skill that will determine more about their life than almost any content they learn. Every morning they push through the stall is a rep that rewires what they believe they can do.

turn2.read: Agreeing and then doing nothing is a different signal than stalling. They know how to perform cooperation now, which means the conversation itself became the escape hatch. The actual starting is still the problem, and now they have learned that a sincere-sounding yes buys them another day. Underneath that is still the same fear of sitting down and finding out the work is too hard, but the avoidance has gotten one layer more sophisticated.

pull.instinct: Back off the expectation because pushing again feels like nagging, but quietly dropping it teaches them that enough yeses eventually dissolve any standard.

turn2.mentorMove: The conversation is no longer sufficient; the start has to happen in your presence, not as punishment but as proof of concept. Move the agreement from words to a witnessed first action so they cannot agree their way out of actually beginning.
holdFirm: The work still happens today, not tomorrow, not after a fresh conversation.
An agreement that produces nothing is not an agreement; it is a postponement, and you are not accepting that anymore.
stayFlexible: You sit nearby for the first five minutes only, not to supervise but to be the launchpad, then you walk away.
They still choose where to start within the assignment.

script.words: I am not mad, and I am not starting over with a lecture. I know you can do this work. That has not changed.

What I want to understand is what happens between saying yes and the work staying untouched. Is it that sitting down still feels too big even when you mean it? Because I need the real answer, not another agreement.

So here is the new plan, and it is smaller on purpose. Right now, while I am standing here, you open it and do the first thing. I am not staying to watch you finish; I just need to see you start. After that you are on your own.

I have high standards for you and I am not lowering them, because I have seen what your brain does when it actually engages and it is genuinely impressive. But a yes that goes nowhere is not something I can keep accepting, so we are going to prove together right now that you can get through the door.

turn2.longGame: What you are teaching right now is that words have to be backed by action, not as a rule you impose but as a thing that is true in every room they will ever walk into. A person who can start hard things, not just agree to them, is someone others trust with real responsibility. That is the person you are building toward.

secondary.note: The stalling also buys back a small pocket of control over a day that feels mapped out for them.

turn1.read: Stalling is almost never laziness. It is usually a kid sitting at the edge of something that feels hard and choosing not to find out yet whether they can do it. Every minute they delay is a minute they have not failed. The schoolwork feels like a test of whether they are capable, and the morning is when that fear is freshest.

pull.instinct: Push harder, add consequences, stand over them until they start, which treats the surface behavior as the problem and makes the desk feel like a place of pressure rather than a place they can succeed.

turn1.mentorMove: Name what you see without making it a character charge, shrink the on-ramp so starting feels survivable, and let them have some say in how the morning is structured so the work is something they step into rather than something that happens to them.
holdFirm: The work gets done every morning, full stop.
The agreement you made together is the agreement.
stayFlexible: What they start with, so they can pick the piece that feels most approachable.
The exact timing and order within the morning block.
Whether they work at the table, on the floor, or somewhere else that helps their brain settle.

script.words: I have noticed mornings have been rough lately and I do not think you are blowing this off on purpose. I think there is something about sitting down to start that feels heavy, and I want to understand that before we figure out the fix.

When you are stalling, what is actually going through your head? Is it that you do not know where to begin, or that you are dreading a specific part, or something else entirely? I am asking for real because the answer changes what we do next.

What if you got to pick which piece you start with every morning? You know this material better than I know what part of it trips you up. If you tell me what makes the launch easier, we can build the morning around that instead of fighting it.

The work itself is not going anywhere, and I am not dropping that. But I am holding you to it because I have watched you push through hard things before and come out the other side knowing you did it. That is the thing I want you to keep adding to.

turn1.longGame: A kid who learns that starting is the hard part, and that they can start anyway, builds something that carries them the rest of their life. The goal is not a compliant morning routine. It is a teenager who knows their own brain well enough to work with it instead of against it.

turn2.read: Agreeing and then doing nothing is a step past the original stall. It means they heard what felt like a reasonable plan and still could not get traction, which tells you the barrier is not the structure of the morning but something closer to a belief that starting will reveal they cannot do it. The agreement was real in the moment and collapsed the second they were alone with the blank page. That is not defiance, that is a kid who is more scared than they are letting on.

pull.instinct: Treat the broken agreement as a trust or attitude problem and come down harder, which layers shame on top of the fear that was already stopping them and makes the next attempt feel even more loaded.

turn2.mentorMove: Move one level up the force ladder to a concrete first action small enough that failure is nearly impossible, and sit alongside them for that first piece, not to supervise but to make the start feel less like stepping off a cliff alone.
holdFirm: The work still happens, today, not tomorrow.
A broken agreement gets named out loud, not quietly swallowed.
stayFlexible: How small the first step is, even one sentence or one problem counts as a real start.
Whether you are in the room with them for the launch, at least for now, until momentum builds.
When in the morning the block happens, if shifting it by an hour changes anything.

script.words: I am not coming in angry. I want to say that first. But something is getting in the way and the plan we made did not touch it, so I need us to be more honest with each other than we were last time.

When you sat down and nothing happened, what was the actual moment right before? Because I do not think you wanted to blow it off. I think something felt impossible and I want to know what that was, specifically.

Here is what I want to try. We pick one piece that is the smallest possible start, I mean embarrassingly small, and I sit with you while you do just that piece. Not to watch you, just to be there. Once that piece is done you can decide whether you keep going or take a breath. I think the wall is right at the beginning and I want to help you get past it just once so you know you can.

I am holding the line on the work itself because I have high standards for you and I genuinely believe you can do this, not someday but right now. What I need from you is one honest answer about what the hardest part actually is, so we are solving the real thing this time.

turn2.longGame: What you are really building here is a kid who can tolerate the discomfort of starting something uncertain without needing the exit of avoidance. That skill is worth more than any single lesson they finish this year. The morning work is just the practice ground.
